fact_checks.observation: Four consecutive 'For Problem' paragraphs preserve task, method, and result order before a final sensitivity-and-memo sentence.
The contents visibly separate preparation, Problems 1-3, Problem 4 extension, sensitivity, strengths and weaknesses, references, and the later memo.
Tourism appeal precedes failure risk, rescue urgency, practical environmental factors, and the first official task.
The remaining official tasks precede 'To address the mentioned issues' and a color-coded workflow, followed immediately by assumptions.
Bold assumptions carry short justifying explanations, then notation gives way to an operational stay-put safety recommendation.
Seabed and vehicle figures are introduced before the coordinate frame and vertical location model.
Newton balance, mass split, buoyancy, drag, and Reynolds relation are each followed by a plain-language definition or caveat.
The completed vertical ODE is followed by a bullet handoff to XY motion, a current map, and relative-current force.
Analytical difficulty motivates RK4; the generic IVP and recurrence precede Step1 initial-state instructions.
Equation conversion and one-second iteration are followed by a bold Results and Analysis heading and the normal-resurfacing case.
The normal case is quantified first, then failed ballast produces seabed and neutral-buoyancy visual branches before uncertainty.
Initial state, currents, and topography are named before transmitted data and six recommended sensors.
Endpoint cases motivate surface, shallow, and deep-water zones before the equipment table and entropy-weight method.
Normalization, probabilities, entropy, weights, benefit/cost aggregation, and the final ratio appear in calculation order.
Figure 8 is introduced before ranking drones and sonar and then qualifying the recommendation with AUV and AUR capabilities.
Grid size, current distributions, ballast distribution, initial depth, 100000 samples, and four endpoint percentages precede the plots.
Trajectory and heatmap interpretations precede the simultaneous surface-and-underwater search recommendation.
Searched points are propagated and removed, then Bayesian updating, cumulative success, urgency, and the initial grid are defined before the flowchart.
Figure 11 precedes the result section; Figure 12 is followed by current-direction and convergence interpretations.
One-, three-, and five-hour starts lead directly to the claim that rescue should be deployed as soon as possible, then to transfer.
Climate/current changes and terrain collisions are discussed before conditional instructions to the remaining vehicles.
The paper compares drag perturbations with 400-m horizontal and 40-m vertical bounds before listing strengths.
Two strengths, two weaknesses, and eight references close the technical paper before the memo.
Recipient, sender, date, subject, risk, model purpose, current-monitoring recommendation, equipment ranking, and search method appear in that order.
Route geometry and urgency are repeated before a three-row probability table, procurement advice, a tourism-safety conclusion, and a courteous closing.

g7_warnings.warning: A red watermark, QR mark, and Chinese footer appear throughout; extraction mojibake must not be treated as positive English evidence.
The rescue objective is not connected to passenger survival windows, medical urgency, or a calibrated detection-to-rescue likelihood.
Stable weather and calm seas are assumed even though currents and delayed rescue are central uncertainty drivers.
Immediate permanent immobilization after seabed contact is asserted from sediment without collision, slope, burial, or rebound evidence.
All rescue equipment is assumed deployable within one hour without mobilization, launch, travel, weather, staffing, or readiness data.
The text recommends staying in place after contact loss but the dynamics section immediately assumes prompt ascent; the operational rule is not reconciled.
Longitude and latitude are used as x and y coordinates without a local metric projection or degree-to-distance conversion.
The fitted seabed surface lacks a stated data resolution, fitting method, residual analysis, and collision-event implementation.
Vehicle mass, volume, area, ballast capacity, speed, and shape parameters are not frozen in a complete sourced table.
Equation 3 mixes z sign convention and g/cm^3 units without a stated validity range or source calibration.
The laminar-flow assumption and a constant empirical Reynolds number are not reconciled with vehicle scale or relative velocities.
Squared relative speed is used without an explicit sign or vector direction, so the force can point the wrong way.
The text says Equations 2-6 produce Equation 6 and later calls Equation 7 the complex vertical equation; numbering references are inconsistent.
Only the x-force is printed explicitly and the y model is declared similar without a complete vector formulation.
The stated O(h^5) truncation error does not distinguish local from global RK4 error.
The generic recurrence shifts between y and z notation and the printed first-order system contains symbol and coefficient ambiguities.
Initial states, physical parameter values, event handling, code, tolerances, random seed, and package versions are absent.
Trajectory figures are not accompanied by a table of final coordinates, surfacing times, seabed-hit times, or uncertainty intervals.
Uniform ballast mass is assumed without minimum, maximum, engineering basis, or a failure-mode probability.
Seabed contact and neutral buoyancy are simulated without an explicit event detector, collision law, or validated ballast mechanism.
Initial state, current, and terrain uncertainties are listed qualitatively but are not propagated from measured error distributions.
The GPS recommendation acknowledges signal blockage but does not specify buoy, acoustic, surfacing, synchronization, or failure architecture.
Table 1 mixes range, precision, accuracy, failure rate, and dollar costs without a frozen source record or consistent units.
Section 6.3 refers to Table 2 although the visible equipment table is numbered Table 1.
The below-versus-above 3000-m wording is ambiguous for depth sign and does not justify the chosen operational boundary.
The prose says larger entropy means more differentiation and should receive higher weight, contradicting the printed 1-e_j weight formula.
The text calls e_j the entropy of the ith index and does not document zero handling, indicator orientation, or the full normalized matrix.
Benefit and normalized cost are divided without a transparent budget, currency year, quantity, lifecycle horizon, or compatibility constraint.
Figure 8 lacks a table of exact scores, uncertainty, alternative weights, and procurement quantities.
The search implementation does not fully connect drones, sonar, AUVs, and AURs to depth-specific coverage and detection probability.
The 400-m grid and 30-by-75 extent are chosen without resolution sensitivity, geographic projection, or explicit search-area bounds.
Current means, variances, correlations, temporal structure, ballast bounds, initial-state errors, and random seed are missing.
Using 100000 samples is described as sufficient without convergence diagnostics or validation against observed drift.
Endpoint proportions and grid frequencies are treated as probabilities without a calibrated observation or detection model.
The position is frozen within each one-hour search cycle despite movement being the principal reason probabilities change.
Event B and P(B|A_i) are not operationally defined for positive, negative, or missed detections.
Equation 22's complement bar is visually present, but independence, detector false negatives, and repeated-coverage dependence are unstated.
The search objective introduces k without units, estimation, sensitivity, or linkage to rescue survival.
Colony size, pheromone parameters, transition rule, stopping tolerance, constraints, route cost, and code are absent.
The paper moves among 12 percent surface success, 63 percent conditional surface coverage, and 43 percent overall success without a closed accounting table.
Figure 12's caption describes probabilities with different t although its panels show a route and iteration result; Figure 13 is captioned as a route although it plots start-time probabilities.
The body reports 43 percent at a one-hour start and about 10 percent at five hours, while the memo table reports 46 percent and 13 percent.
Stronger perturbations, collisions, immediate power loss, and probabilistic mass loss are proposed without equations, parameters, or validation.
The extension is qualitative and omits communication reliability, vehicle assignment, collision avoidance, shared search optimization, and rescue prioritization.
Only drag-coefficient perturbations are shown; a 400-m shift is called harmless despite matching one grid width, and no code, data, environment, or expected outputs support replay.
